title: Rising potassium and creatinine after a new drug: ACE inhibitor (lisinopril)
vignette: A 59-year-old man who is being treated for hypercholesterolemia, diabetes, and hypertension comes to the physician for a scheduled follow-up visit three weeks after starting a new medication. He has no new complaints. Blood work drawn yesterday shows an interim increase in potassium from 4.8 mEq/L to 5.2 mEq/L and a creatinine elevation from 1.2 mg/dL to 1.6 mg/dL. Administration of which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the change in this patient's renal function?

clues.text: increase in potassium from 4.8 mEq/L to 5.2 mEq/L and a creatinine elevation from 1.2 mg/dL to 1.6 mg/dL
clues.note: A modest rise in potassium (5.2 / normal 3.5-5.0) plus creatinine (1.6 / normal 0.6-1.2) after starting a drug is the classic effect of an ACE inhibitor (dilates the efferent arteriole -> lower GFR; reduces aldosterone -> hyperkalemia).

whatMatters: An ACE INHIBITOR (LISINOPRIL) reduces angiotensin II, DILATING the EFFERENT arteriole -> decreased intraglomerular pressure -> lower GFR (rise in creatinine); reduced aldosterone -> HYPERKALEMIA. A modest early rise in K/creatinine is expected. Answer A.
strategy: Match the lab pattern (increased creatinine + hyperkalemia soon after a new antihypertensive) to the drug: ACE inhibitor (lisinopril). Reject drugs that don't cause this pattern: metoprolol (beta blocker, no significant GFR change), atorvastatin (myopathy/hepatotoxicity, not this), hydrochlorothiazide/furosemide (potassium-WASTING diuretics -> hypokalemia), metformin (lactic acidosis risk, not GFR-lowering itself), and prazosin (alpha-1 blocker, no GFR effect).

eliminations.label: Metoprolol - beta blocker, no GFR change
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a beta-1 blocker (reduces heart rate/renin). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it doesn't meaningfully change GFR or cause this creatinine/potassium rise. ✅ Correct if: bradycardia/AV block from a beta blocker.

eliminations.label: Atorvastatin - myopathy/hepatotoxicity
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: its adverse effects are myopathy and transaminitis; it wouldn't cause hyperkalemia/rising creatinine without massive rhabdomyolysis (which would have myalgias, high CK, dark urine). ✅ Correct if: statin myopathy with elevated CK.

eliminations.label: Hydrochlorothiazide - potassium-WASTING
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a thiazide diuretic. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: thiazides cause HYPOkalemia (potassium wasting), the opposite of this hyperkalemia. ✅ Correct if: hypokalemia/hyponatremia/hyperuricemia from a thiazide.

eliminations.label: Furosemide - potassium-WASTING loop diuretic
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a loop diuretic. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it also causes HYPOkalemia, not hyperkalemia. ✅ Correct if: hypokalemia/metabolic alkalosis/ototoxicity from a loop diuretic.

eliminations.label: Metformin - lactic acidosis, not GFR-lowering
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a biguanide for diabetes. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: metformin does not itself lower GFR or raise potassium; its concern is lactic acidosis in renal impairment. ✅ Correct if: lactic acidosis in the setting of renal dysfunction/contrast.

eliminations.label: Prazosin - alpha-1 blocker, no GFR effect
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an alpha-1 antagonist for hypertension/BPH. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it lowers BP by vasodilation but does not decrease GFR or cause hyperkalemia. ✅ Correct if: orthostatic hypotension (first-dose).

reasoning: Three weeks after a new drug, potassium and creatinine rise modestly
ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and GFR (creatinine up)
They also reduce aldosterone, causing potassium retention (hyperkalemia)
mechanism: ANGIOTENSIN-CONVERTING ENZYME (ACE) INHIBITORS (the '-pril' drugs, e.g., LISINOPRIL) block conversion of angiotensin I to ANGIOTENSIN II. Angiotensin II normally constricts the EFFERENT glomerular arteriole more than the afferent, maintaining intraglomerular pressure and GFR; by removing this efferent constriction, ACE inhibitors DECREASE intraglomerular pressure and GFR, producing a modest rise in serum CREATININE (an expected effect, of concern only if creatinine rises >30% or the patient has bilateral renal artery stenosis). Reduced angiotensin II also lowers ALDOSTERONE, decreasing renal potassium excretion and causing HYPERKALEMIA. This gives the classic pattern of a small early increase in creatinine AND potassium after starting therapy (other ACE inhibitor effects: cough from bradykinin, angioedema). The distractors don't produce this pattern: beta blockers, statins, alpha blockers, and metformin don't lower GFR/raise potassium this way, and thiazide/loop diuretics cause potassium WASTING (hypokalemia).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm/Renal > ACE inhibitors: block angiotensin II -> dilate efferent arteriole -> decreased GFR (creatinine up) + decreased aldosterone (hyperkalemia); cough (bradykinin), angioedema; avoid in bilateral renal artery stenosis/pregnancy; renoprotective in diabetic nephropathy.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Rising creatinine + hyperkalemia after new antihypertensive = ACE inhibitor (lisinopril).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on ACE inhibitor, efferent arteriole, GFR, aldosterone, or hyperkalemia? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Thiazide/loop diuretics cause HYPOkalemia; beta/alpha blockers, statin, metformin don't lower GFR/raise K this way.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: ACE inhibitor -> efferent dilation (decreased GFR, creatinine up) + decreased aldosterone (hyperkalemia); cough/angioedema.

keywords.front: Rising creatinine + hyperkalemia after new drug

keywords.back: Dilates efferent arteriole -> lower GFR (creatinine up)

keywords.front: Concerning creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor

firstAid.detail: Pharm > diuretics waste K; beta/alpha blockers, metformin differ.
Renal > avoid ACE inhibitor in bilateral stenosis.

memoryHook: Lisino'-pril' relaxes the exit (efferent) arteriole - pressure drops so GFR falls (creatinine nudges up) and aldosterone dips, so potassium climbs.
